newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African data barrage seen pointing to lower rate.
newsitem.headline: S.African data barrage seen pointing to lower rate.

text.p: South Africa's financial markets are braced for an avalanche of economic indicators next week which should all continue to point the way to lower interest rates, economists said on Friday.
Growth in money supply, private sector credit extension and consumer inflation are all expected to have slowed in June, adding further ammunition to economists' calls for a cut in interest rates.
Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals has stated in the past that he will not relax monetary policy until the three indicators have slowed.
First to kick off the data will be June money supply and private sector credit extension, both due for release by the central bank at 1500 GMT on Monday.
A Reuters consensus poll of economists forecasts that money supply growth rose 14.4 percent year-on-year compared with a preliminary 15.4 percent increase in May.
A high base in June last year coupled with a continuing slowdown in credit extension was behind the slowing trend, economists said.
"Apart from the fact that we are expecting credit to come off, there are technical factors. M3 is basically coming off a high base," Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes said.
The consensus forecast for credit extension is for a 15.19 percent year-on-year rise versus May's 16.57 percent.
But Barnard Jacobs Mellet economist Chantal Friedman said credit extension would rebound on a month-on-month basis from a subdued 0.2 percent May rise, due to seasonal factors.
"While we expect a higher month-on-month rate, the impact of high interest rates and high consumer debt should limit overall growth in this aggregate," she said.
"As with M3, a high base in June 1996 should result in a sharp fall in the year-on-year rate," she added.
Inflation data due for release by the Central Statistical Service at 0900 GMT is expected to show declining prices for the third consecutive month.
Economists forecast June CPI would rise 9.1 percent year-on-year compared with May's 9.5 percent rise.
Friedman said consumer inflation would be limited by a sharp fall in petrol prices in the month.
"The only major quarterly survey in June is furniture and equipment, where prices appear to have been reasonably steady over the second quarter," she added.

But Huysamer Stals economist Johan Rossouw warned that food prices would probably exert upward pressure because of a cold snap at the end of May and a rise in vegetable exports which would have reduced local supplies.
Finally on Friday, the Reserve Bank will release July gold and foreign exchange reserves data at 1600 GMT.
Economists were loathe to forecast the indicator a week before month end, but some said that indications were the figure would be sideways to higher.
Reserves are expected to total between 21.5 billion and 23.3 billion rand, versus 22.1 billion in June.

Edey Rogers economist Hugo Klein said he expected the proceeds of government's $250 million Yankee bond issue in June to be offset by Reserve Bank intervention in the foreign exchange market in the month.

Economists also noted that while foreigners had been net sellers of domestic bonds at one point in the month, the resumption of buying in the latter half of the month would have probably neutralised those outflows.
